newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Big UK fund manager in ABN AMRO's sights.
newsitem.headline: Big UK fund manager in ABN AMRO's sights.

text.p: Expansionary Dutch bank ABN AMRO Holding NV would consider buying a large British fund manager if it fitted in with its strategy, Jan Vroegop, director of ABN AMRO's global asset management department, said on Tuesday.

ABN AMRO has been dragged into the controversy surrounding Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) over the last week by reports that it tried to poach MGAM staff and back a management buy-out of MGAM's British pension fund business.
Vroegop did not mention any targets but said the bank would like to make "big steps" in London funds management.
"If that meant we would have to make an acquisition that fitted in with our strategic plan, we would seriously look at it," he said in a telephone interview.
But he added: "We don't want to be involved in all sorts of competitive bidding for British asset managers because we think the prices on many occasions were too high."
The bank's last two British fund management acquisitions, Causeway Group and Carrington Pembroke, were small and aimed at wealthy private, rather than institutional, clients.
"We don't rule out the possibility we will buy something bigger in the future," Vroegop said.
The Dutch bank has previously denied it tried to lure staff en masse from MGAM.
It has also declined to comment on reports it planned to back a buy-out led by Nicola Horlick, the senior fund manager who resigned from MGAM last week after being suspended.
Noting that ABN AMRO had been speculatively linked with MGAM and the possible purchase of other asset managers, Vroegop said: "That's the fate of a large organisation."
ABN AMRO sees fund management as a core business within its investment banking division and aims to roughly double funds under management to 240 billion guilders within five years.
"That is indeed the strategic goal. You need size in order to be able to remain a fully-fledged organisation that can support all investments," Vroegop said.
But he said the bank did not have in mind a figure for how much it planned to spend on acquisitons.
Managed funds grew 39 percent to 117 billion guilders in 1996, helped by the acquisition last year of Chicago Corp.
ABN AMRO's asset management strategy is to expand activities based around its regional centres of Amsterdam, Chicago and Hong Kong, along with developing a number of local operations.
This included European countries such as Germany and Italy, where state pension systems were being reformed, as well as Latin America, Indonesia and Australia.
But Vroegop said plans to expand the U.S. activities by acquisition had been abandoned because asking prices were too high.
"For the time being, our strategy will be more to develop the business we have in the U.S. and improve the organisation," he said.
Chicago Corp gave the Dutch bank a stronger base which could be developed by bringing in new staff, he said.
